title: Paint House III
summary: There is a row of m houses, each to be painted with one of n colors (labeled from 1 to n), with some houses already painted and thus cannot be repainted.
statement: There is a row of m houses, each to be painted with one of n colors (labeled from 1 to n), with some houses already painted and thus cannot be repainted. A neighborhood is defined as a continuous group of houses painted the same color. Given an array representing the current colors of the houses (where 0 indicates a house that is not yet painted), an m x n matrix of painting costs, and a target number of neighborhoods, determine the minimum cost to paint the remaining houses so that the total number of neighborhoods matches the target. If it is not possible to achieve the target number of neighborhoods, return -1.
constraints: Zero houses are unpainted; positive values are fixed colors 1..n and cost nothing.
A neighborhood is a maximal same-color run; reach exactly target at minimum added cost, or -1.
hints: Memoize by house index, previous color, and neighborhoods formed.
Fixed houses offer one zero-cost color; unpainted houses offer every color with its listed cost.
Increment the group count only when chosen color differs from previous.
The state preserves all history affecting future neighborhoods, and minimizing all legal choices yields the optimum.
editorial: The state preserves all history affecting future neighborhoods, and minimizing all legal choices yields the optimum.

tests.explanation: Painting colors 1,2,2,1,1 costs nine and forms three neighborhoods.
The fixed middle colors permit a minimum-cost exact-three-neighborhood completion.
